Chapter 6: Art, Creation, and the Absurd
There’s a certain magic that happens when someone creates. You know—think about a painter hunched over their canvas late into the night, or a musician just lost in the rhythm of a fresh melody. In those moments, everything else seems to fade away. The absurdity of life? It doesn’t disappear, but it does shift. The artist isn’t really hunting for answers; instead, they’re making something out of nothing, shaping all that chaos into something you can see or hear.
For a lot of us, art becomes a way to actually live with the absurd. It’s not about solving some huge mystery, but about sharing what it feels like to be alive in a world that rarely offers clear explanations. Creation itself turns into a kind of rebellion—a quiet refusal to let the universe’s indifference keep us silent.
Picture a writer, wrestling with doubt, staring at a blank page and wondering if their words even matter. It’s so tempting to just give up. But every sentence, every paragraph, is a little push back against the emptiness. The story that comes out isn’t some perfect answer to the absurd, but it shows just how resilient the human spirit can be.
And here’s something to think about: most people wouldn’t call themselves artists, but in reality, everyone creates in their own way. Maybe it’s a parent making up bedtime stories to comfort their child, or a cook who experiments in the kitchen, turning simple ingredients into something memorable. These everyday acts of creation—they’re all ways of saying yes to life, even when it doesn’t make sense.
Art doesn’t solve the problem of the absurd. But it does give us a way to live with it. Artists know their work might never be finished, that perfection is always just out of reach, and that recognition isn’t guaranteed. But they keep going—not because they’re chasing some big reward, but because the act of creating is a reward all its own.
